Title: Tych testów AI jeszcze nie potrafi zdać. Jeden z nich stworzył Polak

Summary: 
The FrontierMath project, coordinated by Epoch AI, has created a highly difficult mathematics exam for large language models (LLMs). He argues that the future of mathematics will rely on fluid intelligence, creative problem‑solving, and the ability to ask bold questions—skills that machines still lack. The article cites the 50‑problem set, the 4 solved, the 3‑hour time limit, and the one‑million‑token budget as key metrics. It also references the 13‑page solution and the claim that “no current model can figure out how to prove the Riemann hypothesis.”

Title: OpenAI、AIの経済的価値を測る新指標「GDPval」発表　トップ性能はClaude

Summary: 
OpenAI announced a new benchmark called 'GDPval' on 25 September 2025, designed to measure the economic value of AI models by comparing their performance on real‑world tasks to that of human experts. The test draws tasks from 44 occupations spanning the nine U.S. GDP‑contributing sectors and includes 1,320 expert‑crafted tasks, 220 of which are open‑source. Tasks require multimodal outputs such as code, legal briefs, engineering drawings, and customer‑support transcripts, and are scored blind against human‑generated artifacts. In the first round, OpenAI’s GPT‑5 and GPT‑4o, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.1, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro and xAI’s Grok 4 were evaluated. Claude Opus 4.1 achieved the highest score, with 'equal or better' performance on roughly 50 % of tasks. Over the past year, OpenAI’s models have shown near‑linear gains, with GPT‑5’s GDPval performance more than tripling compared to GPT‑4o, and a two‑fold improvement since spring 2024. The benchmark also revealed that frontier models can complete GDPval tasks about 100 times faster and 100 times cheaper than human experts, even though the tests exclude the human oversight required in real workplaces. OpenAI says GDPval will help ground future AI‑improvement discussions in evidence rather than speculation.

Citation key: [7]
Title: The AI doctor is not ready to see you now: Stress tests reveal flaws

Summary: 
A study published on arXiv (2025) titled 'The Illusion of Readiness: Stress Testing Large Frontier Models on Multimodal Medical Benchmarks' reveals that top-performing multimodal medical AI systems exhibit brittle behavior despite high benchmark scores. Researchers evaluated six flagship models—GPT-5, Gemini-2.5 Pro, OpenAI-o3, OpenAI-o4-mini, and GPT-4o—across six multimodal medical benchmarks, including filtered JAMA (1,141 items), filtered NEJM (743 items), a clinician-curated NEJM subset requiring visual input (175 items), and a visual-substitution set (40 items). Stress tests exposed critical vulnerabilities: removing image inputs caused significant accuracy drops, especially on NEJM, where GPT-4o fell from 66.90% to 37.28%. On the NEJM visual-subset, GPT-4o scored only 3.4% without images, while others remained above the 20% random baseline. Format manipulations—such as randomizing answer options—reduced text-only accuracy (e.g., GPT-5: 37.71% → 32.00%) while image+text performance remained stable or improved. Distractor replacement caused text-only accuracy to decline toward chance, with GPT-5 dropping to 20.00% at 4R, while image+text accuracy rose to 90.86%. Visual substitution trials, where images were replaced with distractor-aligned alternatives, caused accuracy collapses: GPT-5 dropped from 83.33% to 51.67%. Chain-of-thought reasoning reduced accuracy on NEJM and VQA-RAD, with minor gains only for o4-mini. Audits found incorrect logic paired with correct answers, hallucinated visual details, and stepwise descriptions that did not guide decisions. The authors warn that high benchmark scores mask brittle behavior, shortcut learning, and fabricated reasoning, and urge systematic stress testing, detailed benchmark documentation, and robustness metrics to align AI progress with clinical trust and safety.

Published date: October 07 2025, 13:30

Title: AI systems are great at tests. But how do they perform in real life?

Summary: 
The article discusses how current AI evaluation relies heavily on benchmark tests, which may not reflect real‑world performance. It cites OpenAI’s claim that GPT‑5 is "much smarter across the board" and notes that high benchmark scores have led to significant funding, such as Cognition AI’s $175 million raise after a software‑engineering benchmark. The piece highlights that benchmarks can be gamed, citing Meta’s optimisation of Llama‑4 for a chatbot‑ranking site and OpenAI’s use of the FrontierMath dataset, illustrating Goodhart’s law: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Rumman Chowdhury warns that over‑emphasis on metrics can lead to "manipulation, gaming, and a myopic focus on short‑term qualities and inadequate consideration of long‑term consequences". The article argues for more holistic evaluation frameworks, such as MedHELM, which uses 35 benchmarks across five clinical categories to better mimic real‑world medical tasks. It calls for a new evaluation ecosystem that incorporates red‑team testing and field testing to assess AI’s broader economic, cultural, and societal impacts.
